steps.voiceover: Everything starts at the "+ Create" launcher, reachable from the sidebar on every page. It offers four equally-ranked ways in: describe what you need in plain language, start from a ready-made setup, build it yourself on a canvas, or spin up a single assistant to chat with. None is a forced default, and the titles avoid our internal vocabulary — you choose by what you want to do. For the demo we take "Start from a ready-made setup".

The wizard lands on the Process step — the template gallery. It comes first on purpose, because it's the central decision. For the demo we pick a ready-made template, the Core SDLC flow. It gives us four agents that cover a full build-and-review loop: a Business Analyst who writes issues, a Developer who implements them, a Code Reviewer, and a Reworker. The live preview on the right confirms the hand-offs connect.
Next, the working environment — where the team operates. It bundles the repository, the branch, and the credentials into one reusable template, so we just pick one from the grid.
Step three gives the team its identity: a name and an ID, both pre-filled from the environment. The ID becomes the prefix for every agent the team creates, like agentic-demos-developer.
Knowledge is optional. Here we choose the skills every member inherits, the sources it can query at runtime, and how learnings are shared across the team. We accept the defaults.
Finally, review — everything in one place. When we hit create, the wizard builds the whole team in one atomic transaction, each member with its own chat identity, ready for the first issue.

chapters.title: The IBAN Story — the label-driven SDLC loop

steps.voiceover: This is the Agent Chat, where a human talks directly to any agent. On the left is our team with its four members: Business Analyst, Code Reviewer, Developer and Reworker. In the middle is the conversation, and on the right a live view into the agent's own workspace.

I describe the request to the Business Analyst in plain language. Here's the first thing to appreciate: it doesn't just start writing a spec. It looks at the current form and pushes back with the six questions that genuinely need a human decision — when validation happens, what to do on an invalid IBAN, what if the service is down. I answer point by point, steering the outcome without writing a requirements document myself.

With my decisions, the Business Analyst files the issue in GitHub. It's written in two layers: a plain-language human section any stakeholder can read, and a full agent section with the problem, scope, and numbered, testable acceptance criteria for the delivery team.

The ready-for-implementation label fired a trigger, and the Developer woke up automatically — no one opened this chat to prompt it. It implemented the whole change on its own: a testable client, the validation states wired into the form, passing tests, a green build — then opened a pull request and labelled it ready-for-review. The Developer never reviews or merges its own work.

Same pattern again: the ready-for-review label woke the Code Reviewer. It checked out the branch, reviewed the full diff in context, and went through the acceptance criteria one by one. Its verdict: all met, tests pass, build green — and it applies ready-to-merge, noting that a human performs the merge.

The most intuitive kind is a scheduled trigger. I pick Cron, choose Daily at 07:00 — the platform confirms it in plain language and shows the cron expression — and write the prompt the agent runs every morning, unattended.
The simplest type is Once — a one-shot that fires a single time at a moment you pick, then removes itself. Here it delivers a personal reminder.

An HTTP webhook lets an external system fire the trigger. The panel generates a dedicated endpoint and a required secret — copy it once into your calling system; there's no open, unauthenticated mode.

This is the type doing the real work in a flow. I pick the repository and one event from the full catalog — here Issue labeled — and narrow it to a single label, "ready", so the agent reacts to precisely the signal it cares about.

The subtlest type is a data-flow dependency. It reframes a push as a hand-off between teammates: an upstream agent committed its work, so now it's your turn. The woken agent pulls, checks relevance, and continues — or replies PASS.
A draft is an editable process that exists before any team is created — nothing is live, nothing spawned. Here's a fresh, empty one called Simple SDLC. Let's add our first agent.
I click Add agent and choose "From scratch". Instead of writing a system prompt by hand, I give the agent a name and jot down one line of intent: take requirements and create a GitHub issue.

Here's where we are: two agents on the canvas, each with its generated prompt — but standing side by side, unconnected. Two agents that don't hand work to each other aren't a process yet. The next step makes it a flow.

I drag from the Business Analyst's port onto the Developer and choose an Issue channel: the BA opens an issue that wakes the Developer. I add a routing label, "ready", and tick the human approval gate — so the Developer only starts once a person applies that label. And there it is: a working, human-gated flow.

As a final touch I turn on Stages, and the flow organises into labelled bands — Requirements holding the BA, Build holding the Developer. From here, one click on Materialize would turn this drawing into a live, running team. That's the whole story of Flows: design it visually, and go live only when you're ready.

This is the Knowledge Flow page. The page itself stays lean — title, counts, and the team's knowledge flow. The whole model lives one click away, behind the question mark: Memory is what one agent privately remembers, Knowledge is what the team shares, and Skills are the reusable instruction files distilled from the best of it. The help panel walks the three stages, and the control surface that decides how much happens automatically.

We pick a team, and the page draws its whole knowledge flow left to right: the agents on the left, the shared team knowledge they feed in the middle, and the skills on the right. A brand-new team hasn't learned anything yet — which is exactly the point: you watch this fill in as the team works.

The end of the pipeline is skills. Here we take a reusable skill from the pool and activate it on the team. Activation is an immediate file sync — no restart — and the inspector confirms it reached every member's workspace, not just a team-level toggle. That's the same one-click control you use to promote a team's own learned knowledge into a skill.

We narrow the Team filter to one team and open up the range to all time. The summary cards show the totals — input, output, cache — the chart plots tokens per day, and the table breaks the spend down by agent.
The Group by control re-keys the breakdown table on demand — here, by team, folding every agent's spend into one row.
